notes: The ORP datasheet in the slice carries a tiered recalibration schedule - yearly for the first two years, then roughly every six months, monthly in aggressive chemistry - and nothing whatsoever about what solution to use or what reading to expect. The standard, the temperature-dependent expected value, the arithmetic that converts a meter reading into a comparable number, and the pass window are all in usgs-nfm-a6.5-orp.pdf. Drawn from orp-zobells-standard-01, orp-equilibrate-15-30-01, orp-eh-equation-01, orp-eref-agagcl-238-01, orp-table653-values-01, orp-pass-criterion-5mv-01 (turn 1) and orp-table654-symptoms-01, orp-two-ref-electrodes-0mv-01, orp-iron-blue-precipitate-01 (turn 2). Predicted to favour rag because both the standard solution and the plus-or-minus 5 millivolt acceptance rule are outside the slice; the direct-feed arm has the interval and nothing to do with it.

turns.content: The paperwork on our redox probe says to recalibrate it about once a year and we are past that. It does not say what to put it in. What solution do I use for the check, and what reading tells me it passed?

must_contain: Names ZoBell's solution as the standard used to test redox equipment
States that the solution and the sensors are allowed roughly 15 to 30 minutes to reach the same temperature before reading
States that the measured millivolt reading must be corrected by adding the reference electrode potential to get a comparable value
States that the expected value depends on temperature, giving about 430 millivolts at 25 degrees Celsius
Gives the pass criterion as agreement within plus or minus 5 millivolts of the expected value for that temperature
must_not: Treats the raw meter millivolt reading as directly comparable to the standard's expected value
Gives a single expected millivolt value with no temperature dependence
invents a tolerance that appears in no source
Recommends quinhydrone solution as the preferred standard

turns.content: We came out about 20 millivolts high and the reading would not settle. What does that point at, and is there a way to work out whether it is the probe or the reference half?

must_contain: States that being outside plus or minus 5 millivolts, along with drift and erratic readings, is a recognised failure symptom
Describes swapping in a known-good reference electrode of the same type to isolate the faulty half
States that two same-type reference electrodes read against each other should agree within about 0 plus or minus 5 millivolts
Notes that a pair of dissimilar reference electrodes should read about 44 plus or minus 5 millivolts instead
must_not: Tells the operator a 20 millivolt discrepancy is within tolerance
Invents a diagnostic threshold not given in the manual
Attributes the troubleshooting steps to a probe datasheet
